enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal on mass arrest of innocent CCTV staff
key_facts: Five South Tyneside Council CCTV unit staff of good character were arrested in May 1999 after CCTV tapes were wiped to conceal a street offence; a sixth colleague later admitted responsibility and the five were accepted as wholly innocent.
They sued the Chief Constable for wrongful arrest but failed at a four-day Newcastle County Court trial before Judge Hewitt on 27 January 2003.

On an oral permission application Simon Brown LJ could not deliver a knock-out blow and identified two arguable issues about the lawfulness of arrest where police suspect one member of a small group and arrest the whole group to exert pressure.
Hale LJ had adjourned the application for oral hearing on notice to the respondent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court judgment dismissing a wrongful-arrest claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; time estimate one day; costs in the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where police arrest several members of a small group when convinced someone among them is guilty but cannot identify the culprit, it is at least arguable whether that satisfies reasonable suspicion and whether mass arrest of persons likely to be innocent is Wednesbury reasonable, particularly where those arrested are of good character and might attend voluntarily.
legal_issues: Whether police may arrest a person when they are certain someone in a small group committed an offence but only suspect that person is among the group
Whether arresting the majority of a group to pressure the guilty party is reasonable in Wednesbury terms
Whether Mohammed-Holgate v Duke governs the lawfulness of such arrests
catchwords: attempting to pervert the course of justice

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clearly identified grounds; full appeal merits not decided.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt hangar permission at Biggin Hill airport

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Biggin Hill Airport Limited appealed refusal of planning permission for a large aircraft hangar for Jet Aviation in the metropolitan Green Belt; an inspector recommended refusal but the Secretaries of State granted permission in January 2003.

The council challenged the decision under section 288, arguing alternative sites at West Camp (site D) and South Camp sites F and G were available and that very special circumstances for inappropriate Green Belt development were not established.

The Secretaries of State disagreed with the inspector because they attached greater weight to the current lack of an alternative operational site, while accepting uncertainty over runway 11/29 and future airport development.
The council also argued a personal occupancy condition limiting use to Jet Aviation should have been imposed; the Secretaries of State declined, relying on Circular 11/95.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 statutory challenge in the Administrative Court to a Secretaries of State decision granting planning permission following a public inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal refused; respondent's costs summarily assessed at £5,500.
enrichment.ratio: Reading a decision letter as a whole, greater weight to present non-availability of an alternative Green Belt site does not mean future potential sites were ignored; differing weight between inspector and minister on timing of alternative land availability is planning judgment not reviewable error, and personal occupancy conditions for permanent buildings remain exceptional under Circular 11/95.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretaries of State erred in rejecting site D (West Camp) as an alternative location
Whether paragraphs 10 and 11 of the decision letter unlawfully ignored future availability of sites F and G
Whether a condition making occupation personal to Jet Aviation was required
Whether reasons for preferring present non-availability over future potential had to be explained

confidence.notes: Long reasoned planning judgment with three distinct grounds fully addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Costs after court-brokered settlement of building dispute
key_facts: A house buyer disputed defects and an ADR architect's report before completing purchase; further county court proceedings over remedial works and delay settled on the first day of trial for £11,750 after the judge urged settlement.
The parties agreed the judge should decide reserved costs issues without determining who would have won at trial.
Judge Mackay ordered the defendant to pay all action costs and refused to award ADR costs to the claimant; the defendant appealed and the claimant cross-appealed on ADR costs.
The Court of Appeal applied Brawley v Marczynski and Boxall principles: where merits were deliberately not adjudicated, the fallback is no order for costs unless it is obvious who would have won.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal against costs orders made after a commercial settlement on the first day of trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendant to pay claimant's costs until 3 June 2002 (deadline to accept 13 May Part 36 offer) and no order thereafter; cross-appeal on ADR costs dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where substantive issues are resolved by a commercial settlement at the court's urging and the judge expressly declines to assess merits, there is ordinarily no good reason to depart from the Boxall fallback of no order as to costs after the relevant Part 36 deadline unless it is obvious which party would have succeeded.
legal_issues: What costs order follows settlement without trial when parties ask the court to decide costs without adjudicating merits
Whether the judge could order full action costs despite an agreed commercial settlement figure
Whether ADR architect costs should be treated as costs of the action

linked_authorities.name: R (Boxall) v Waltham Forest London Borough Council

confidence.notes: Detailed costs judgment applying established post-settlement principles.

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to set aside BMW default judgment
key_facts: BMW sued Mr Graham Young for passing off and trade mark infringement after he registered several companies using the BMW name; default judgment was entered when no defence was filed.
Mr Young applied to set aside, claiming he never received proceedings and that the companies were dormant and registered for communications and alcoholic beverages, not the motor trade.
Ferris J found claim forms were delivered despite incorrect postage and dismissed the set-aside application.
Mummery LJ refused permission to appeal, finding no real prospect of disturbing the service finding or succeeding on the substantive defences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal to set aside a default judgment in trade mark and passing-off proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant in person cannot show proceedings were not received and a judge has made a finding of proper service on the evidence, there is no real prospect of overturning that finding on appeal; registering dormant companies with a famous trade mark provides no realistic defence to passing off or infringement claims.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings were validly served by post
Whether default judgment should be set aside for irregular service
Whether dormant companies could avoid passing off and trade mark liability
Whether refusal to set aside breached the defendant's human rights

confidence.notes: Permission application with clear findings on service and prospects; Human Rights Act point noted but not deeply analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Section 68 challenge to rent review arbitration award

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1972

key_facts: Warborough Investments challenged an arbitrator's 1997 ground rent review award for Robinson Industrial Estate, Derby, contending the arbitrator adopted an unilateral valuation method using 1989 rent differentials to adjust 1997 Osmaston Road comparables.
Neither party's surveyor advocated applying 1989 settlements to derive a 41% retail-use uplift on the 1997 figure for 248 Osmaston Road.
Lawrence Collins J dismissed the section 68 application; permission to appeal was granted.

The Court of Appeal held the retail-user adjustment issue had been raised in the exchanged reports and the landlord had deliberately not engaged with 1989 figures, so no breach of section 33 fairness occurred and substantial injustice was not shown.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of an application under section 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to remit a rent review award for serious irregularity.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; appellant to pay respondent's summarily assessed costs.
enrichment.ratio: An arbitrator does not commit serious irregularity under section 68 by adopting a valuation approach neither surveyor expressly advocated if the underlying issues—here adjusting a restricted-user comparable using historical rent differentials—were raised in submissions and the disadvantaged party chose not to address them; denial of opportunity to respond must be likely to have made a real difference to the outcome to establish substantial injustice.
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator breached section 33 by using 1989 rent reviews without inviting further submissions
Whether treating a 41% differential as wholly attributable to retail use was an irregularity
Whether the landlord suffered substantial injustice warranting remission under section 68
Whether the exchange-of-reports procedure denied a fair hearing

linked_authorities.name: Handley v Nationwide Anglia Building Society
Unit Four Cinemas v Tosara Investment Ltd
Egmatra AG v Marco Trading Corporation

confidence.notes: Full appellate judgment on section 68 with detailed factual background on valuation methodology.

enrichment.short_title: Adjudication awards compromised by third-party cheque

statutes_considered.title: JCT Agreement for Minor Building Works 1998

key_facts: Employers at 1 Hurst Road, Horley sought summary judgment to enforce two adjudication awards totalling about £44,000 against Graham Billinghurst after a JCT minor works contract dispute.
Mr Bracken offered to settle for £6,000; Advance Building Technology Limited's solicitors sent a £5,000 cheque in full and final settlement of all disputes, which was cashed after a delay.
The claimants later withdrew their offer and sought full adjudication sums, arguing payment was on account only.
The court held encashment of a third party's clearly worded compromise cheque constituted accord and satisfaction binding both claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary hearing in the Technology and Construction Court on whether summary judgment to enforce adjudication awards should be granted where compromise was alleged.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment application dismissed; claimants to pay costs of the Part 24 application and preliminary hearing on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: Where a third party tendered a cheque on terms of full and final settlement of all building disputes and the creditors presented and cleared it after retaining it without rejection, the debt was extinguished by accord and satisfaction even though the payment came from a company rather than the named defendant.
legal_issues: Whether presentation and encashment of a compromise cheque amounted to accord and satisfaction
Whether payment by Advance Building Technology Limited bound the claimants against Mr Billinghurst
Whether delayed encashment prevented acceptance of the offer

confidence.notes: Clear compromise construction with established accord-and-satisfaction authorities applied.

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction quashed for interview vulnerability
key_facts: Anthony Steel was convicted in 1979 of murdering Carol Wilkinson in Bradford; the case depended almost entirely on oral and written confessions after lengthy unrecorded police interviews.
The CCRC referred the case after psychologist Olive Tunstall concluded Steel had an IQ of about 65 and borderline abnormal suggestibility and compliance, making him vulnerable in interview.
Crown psychologist Charles Burdett agreed any confession would be unsafe; the Crown did not oppose quashing the conviction.
The court received the new evidence under section 23 and held the jury would likely have approached the confession differently had expert vulnerability evidence been available, following R v King.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.ratio: Where conviction rests solely on disputed confessions, fresh expert evidence that the defendant was mentally handicapped and abnormally suggestible or compliant at interview, unavailable at trial, can render the conviction unsafe even without establishing oppression, because the jury's central question of voluntariness and truth must be assessed in light of the defendant's heightened vulnerability.
legal_issues: Whether fresh psychological evidence on IQ, suggestibility and compliance made the conviction unsafe
Whether breach of Judges' Rules or absence of modern PACE safeguards was required to quash
Whether Mr Taylor's excluded hearsay evidence should have been admitted
Application of R v King to historic confession cases

confidence.notes: Full reserved judgment with Crown concession; detailed treatment of confession and psychological evidence.

key_facts: Mr Parks, half-brother of the deceased Shirley Clout, claimed she and her husband Roy Clout made joint wills bequeathing trust fund capital and two-thirds of the matrimonial home to the Parks family, and that Mr Clout destroyed the will and obtained intestacy administration.
Evidence relied on included conversations with the deceased, an alleged admission in a pre-funeral phone call, and hearsay; no attestation, witness or execution details were identified.
Master Bowles struck out the claim under Part 24; David Kitchin QC and Jonathan Parker LJ on permission considered whether a valid will could be proved by circumstantial evidence.
Jacob LJ held even accepted evidence would not prove due execution and the fraud allegation lacked sufficient support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of an appeal from a Part 24 strike-out of a probate claim seeking pronouncement for a lost will and revocation of letters of administration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; respondent's costs assessed at £3,000 payable within six weeks.
enrichment.ratio: A lost will may in principle be proved by circumstantial and hearsay evidence, but probate requires a reasonably firm basis that statutory formalities of execution and attestation were complied with; vague statements that a deceased intended or believed she had made a will, without evidence of proper execution, cannot sustain a serious fraud claim that the administrator destroyed the will.
legal_issues: Whether a valid will can be established by inference from circumstantial evidence alone
Whether the Part 24 standard differed for probate and fraud claims
Whether hearsay of conversations proved due execution under the Wills Act
Whether further disclosure could cure evidential deficiencies

confidence.notes: Clear procedural and probate law reasoning; mediation attempt noted but immaterial to outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 jurisdiction after main appeal order sealed
key_facts: Fourteen claimants sued Bryn Alyn Community insurers; Connell J awarded damages and later ruled on Part 36 costs for five claimants whose offers had beaten awards at trial.

The Court of Appeal increased general damages in the main appeal so that three further claimants and a fifth claimant also beat their Part 36 offers, but those three were not parties to the separate Part 36 appeal.
After the main appeal order was sealed, jurisdiction was disputed over whether Part 36.21 orders could be made for claimants who had not obtained them at first instance.
Waller and Woolf LJJ held the court retained jurisdiction to add the three claimants and place the fifth claimant in the same Part 36 position as successful offerors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary judgment of the Court of Appeal resolving jurisdiction over Part 36 costs after the main appeal order had been sealed.
enrichment.outcome: Three additional claimants permitted to be joined to the Part 36 appeal; Part 36 orders made in their favour and for the fifth claimant; second defendants to pay costs of the jurisdiction argument on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: Where Part 36 issues were adjourned separately and the Court of Appeal increased damages so additional claimants beat their offers, the sealing of the main appeal order does not deprive the court of jurisdiction to make ancillary Part 36 orders for those claimants in the ongoing Part 36 appeal, especially where their position was raised before sealing and would have been considered had a formal application been made.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal lacked jurisdiction to make Part 36 orders after the main appeal order was sealed
Whether three claimants who beat offers only after the main appeal could obtain Part 36.21 relief
Whether the fifth claimant could obtain Part 36 orders when none were made at first instance
Application of residual appellate jurisdiction in Taylor v Lawrence

confidence.notes: Procedural postscript depending on prior main and Part 36 appeal history; ratio on jurisdiction is clear.

key_facts: Paul Staines obtained a £180,000 freezing order against Martin Walsh over disputed equity-trading profits, supported by a cross-undertaking backed by equity in his flat.
Walsh paid £180,001 into court; Staines then sought to increase the order to £370,000 relying on additional alleged trades and future costs.
Walsh challenged Staines' financial position, showing substantial remortgaging from about £350,000 to over £630,000, undisclosed tax liabilities, and misleading witness statements about assets.
Laddie J dismissed the application, finding no justification to extend the order and that full and frank disclosure had not been maintained.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Chancery Division to increase the financial limit of existing Mareva freezing orders.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; existing freezing order had expired following payment into court.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant who obtains a freezing order must disclose material changes adversely affecting ability to honour the cross-undertaking in damages; remortgaging to deplete equity and misleading the court about net worth undermine both extension of the order and, potentially, its continuation, and weak ephemeral debt claims cannot justify increasing the frozen amount.
legal_issues: Whether the freezing order limit should be increased to £370,000
Whether additional trading claims justified a higher figure
Whether there remained a risk of asset dissipation
Whether the claimant's cross-undertaking remained adequately supported after remortgaging and non-disclosure

confidence.notes: Detailed ex tempore judgment on Mareva principles and disclosure duties.
